items.q: Which exit should I take at Alexanderplatz station?
items.a: **Follow `Ausgang Dircksenstraße` for the World Clock and the open square, and `Ausgang Rathausstraße` for the TV Tower and the Rotes Rathaus.** Those two cover almost every visitor reason for being at this station. From Rathausstraße the TV Tower entrance is 183 metres; from Grunerstraße, the traffic side, it is 358 metres and you have a wide road to cross. Grunerstraße is worth taking only for the Alexa shopping centre.

items.q: What does Ausgang mean on a Berlin station sign?
items.a: **`Ausgang` means exit.** The useful part is the word that follows it, which in Berlin is a street name: `Ausgang Kantstraße`, `Ausgang Leipziger Platz`. Some exits also carry a letter, but letters get covered during building work and Berlin always has building work, so **treat the street name as the real label** and the letter as a bonus.

items.q: Which exit at Zoologischer Garten is closest to the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church?
items.a: **Kantstraße, at 55 metres.** This is the biggest exit penalty in central Berlin: the Hardenbergplatz exits leave you 256 metres away on the far side of a bus station and a wide road, so the wrong choice costs you around 200 metres and three extra minutes. Zoologischer Garten has 13 exits spread over 307 metres, the widest spread of any central Berlin station.

items.q: Which exit do I take for Berlin Zoo?
items.a: **It depends on which gate you are using, and the two are 400 metres apart.** `Ausgang Hardenbergplatz` is the side for the Löwentor, the Lion Gate that opened in 1909. `Ausgang Budapester Straße` is the side for the Elefantentor, the ornate 1899 Elephant Gate that appears on the postcards. Both gates sell tickets, so decide the gate first and let it choose your exit.

items.q: Does BVG publish a map of station exits?
items.a: **No. The BVG station pages give you departures, lines and lift information, but no exit map.** The letters and street names live on the walls underground and almost nowhere online, which is exactly why visitors surface on the wrong side so often. That gap is why I built the Berlin Station Exit Map tool from open station entrance data.

items.q: What should I do if I come out of the wrong exit?
items.a: **Stay above ground.** From the street you can see where you are; underground you would be guessing again. Find the nearest street sign, which in Berlin is mounted on the corner of a building rather than on a post, and match it to your map. The one exception is a station where a main road or a rail viaduct really does split the two sides, which is the case at Alexanderplatz between Grunerstraße and the square, and at Zoologischer Garten between Kantstraße and Hardenbergplatz. There, going back down to the concourse can genuinely be shorter.
